title: Big super, banks bet big on AI to roll out cut-price financial advice
full_text:
A chronic shortage of financial advisers coupled with the transformative potential of AI technology means digital financial advice is likely to become the new reality for everyday investors.
New moves by major financial players such as AustralianSuper and the Commonwealth Bank to provide advice have one key factor in common: they utilise AI-backed solutions. It will be the only way these providers can offer advice at competitive prices to the mass market.
Engulfed by red tape and compliance costs, there is now little chance the traditional face-to-face financial advice sector is going to grow – the total number of advisers has halved to around 15,000 over the past decade.
Industry analyst Colin Williams from Padua Wealth offered a bear-case scenario in a recent report, suggesting there may even be fewer advisers by 2030 than there are today.
In any event, the annual costs of full-service financial advice have pushed traditional advice beyond the reach of most people.
But just as prospects looked grim, industry experts suggest Australia is ripe for a hybrid model of human and AI-driven adviser technology that can bridge the so-called “advice gap”.
Behind the headlines of a shrinking advice market is the reality that rising demand for advice from older and wealthier Australians is creating a standout business opportunity.
What’s more, the readiness of the local industry to adopt AI is beyond question; a recent Adviser Ratings survey said 72 per cent of advisers use AI, representing the highest adoption rate in the world.
A new report from consultancy firm Roland Berger found that while AI won’t replace financial advisers, it will “reshape the standards for scale, profitability and competitive advantage throughout the Australian wealth industry”.
Roland Berger partner Ronan Gilhawley makes the point that while the headlines suggest the advisory sector is struggling, major investors with deep pockets have been taking big bets on the power of AI-driven technology to transform industry profitability through recent takeovers.
In the space of a few months CC Capital has made a successful $3bn bid for Insignia (owner of advisory group Shadforth) while Bain Capital has bought Perpetual Wealth.
“What global companies see in Australia is that the potential market is expanding, millions of previously underserved Australians now represent accessible demand thanks to AI-powered services,” Gilhawley says.
Associate wealth editor James Kirby joins wealth editor Julie-Anne Sprague to explain how to find a financial adviser.
In many ways, it is already clear the top end of the market will look after itself: face-to-face financial advice service costing $5000 a year makes sense at this level because of the high net worth of the individual investors concerned.
Boutique advice firms at this level of the market, represented by the annual Barron’s Top 150 Advisers List, would seem secure.
But what is the future for everyone else?
For mum-and-dad investors who occupy the middle tier, there is now a real possibility that AI can transform productivity for traditional advisers. On Gilhawley’s numbers, these advisers can grow their client lists from around 120 per head on average to 150 or more by optimising AI tools for routine tasks and compliance.
But the major change may come in the long-promised provision of low-cost mass advice by the market’s biggest players, especially super funds.
Last year, after signalling it would move back into wealth management, CBA tied up a deal with AI giant OpenAI. This week AustralianSuper, the biggest fund in the local market, registered a new unit, AustralianSuper Advice, where the $410bn fund is taking steps to provide wider financial advice to its customers.
“The big funds have to offer better service, and they have to stem the outflows at the same time,” Gilhawley says.
“We have at least 2.6 million people who want advice, but they can’t afford it. I think we will see a hybrid advice model coming down the line, and at its best we will see much richer offerings than the vastly simplified financial advice we have seen so far.”
